synopsis: Owen Rusk has spent nine years keeping other people's records true. He is a copy clerk at the Registry of Continuant Works in Docketford, where the Count sets the water, the maintenance fund, and the standing of every household. A district lives by its return: one adult to a branch, each speaking only for their own premises, every act supported by two witnesses. A district that cannot perform loses its standing; its people cannot be licensed to trade, have a birth acknowledged or a death entered, or witness anything that matters. The Office does not have to lie. It only has to be accurate. Then a transfer sheet comes up from the seal stair. Lower Lock's crossing, pump, and granary have been moved to the Mill Ward annex. The transfer is dated two days before the receipt is stamped; the ward's vote is recorded as consent, not performance; the crossing lapses. His sister Ada speaks for the ward. She does not need an explanation. She needs him to perform the duty and find two witnesses from outside a ward with no supported district. Owen files the return with a Registry clerk and a Mill Ward counter clerk, who sign only what they have seen. The ward keeps a crossing alive for a document that binds no one at the Office. The Office moves him to a tray of unrouteable post, letters for people it cannot find. He becomes a Continuance Examiner of the Count and learns how the Count works: a reason is a figure, a schedule can outlive the place it names, and a place can be struck on a correct number. Behind it all is the Provisional Mandate. When it ends, the only instrument that can carry the common future is the Common Return, Form Zero, and it has no valid signature path. Every clerk has a copy of the first page in a drawer; nobody has filled it in. Without it, Vespera loses its common future; only what local hands keep alive will endure for a time. To make it real, Owen must build the return from the bottom up, one adult branch at a time, with every name given by the person it belongs to. Standing in his way is not a conspiracy but a building. Halden Pike, the Deputy Registrar, can suspend sixteen districts with one order without telling a lie. The Council answers with circulars; every rule is technically correct. It costs him his post, his place in his sister's ward, and the forgiveness of Nell Arbour, who taught him what a filing is. To save the ward, he must stop certifying other people's acts and become the clerk who asks them to certify their own.

In Saint Vess, a ledger entry can break a fever. A clerk writes the entry, lays the page on an iron plate, and a stranger's fever goes down in a house he has never visited. The charge falls on a pledged year or on a named night. The entry binds only the person who has been told of it, so every reading is public. The interest cannot be paid in coin. It comes out of memory: whole seasons of a remembered life, taken oldest first, or single nights, chosen by the Order and held by the drawer. Corin Hale is a second-desk clerk in the Lower Wharf sub-office. He is twenty-three, earns nine marks a month, and has worked the desk for six years; for two of them he has drawn against the years of his own twenties without ever reading line five. Then he finds a standing order in his own hand and under his own seal, dated eleven months back, that will charge forty marks a season against the ten winters pledged by his sister Nell, a nineteen-year-old lamp mender with three hundred marks due at the Feast sitting. He has no memory of writing it. The page is sealed, and a sealed page cannot be withdrawn. His first move is a public reading, which costs a season and a day and thirteen marks before it reads anything at all. The Order of Stamped Worth has an answer for him. Prior Ysabet Vole offers to lift Nell's pledge outright if Corin will let the account stay unread. The Assay Bench of the Harbour Assize, the one office that could countersign his challenge to the order, has been closed for twelve years. And the appraisal that takes Nell's seasons bears the name of Oriel Brass, the counting-master who taught Corin the desk, while her arrears sit in the same quarter's return under Brass's name. That is the one flaw Corin can prove. The small debt is the least of it. The harbour itself is kept open by a season taken every twelfth month from two hundred and nine accounts, and no one outside the Order has ever been told. Corin has already taken two nights of his mother's memory without knowing it, and he holds the answer to a question Nell has been asking for four years. To clear his sister he can take Vole's offer and let the ledger stay quiet, or he can spend what is left of his own memory and the nights of the people he loves to make Saint Vess read the true account. The Feast is the collection date, and it cannot be moved.

The East Spur tunnel is stable on paper. Marek Venn is a civil engineer for Marrowgate Public Works. He has spent his career making paper agree with stone: a seam on a plan, a load on a shore, a sentence on a form other people must sign. When he finds a mineral seam the surface survey does not show, he refuses to sign Form 7-B. The form would leave the North Relief Branch's repair unowned and reopen the East Spur for a single shift. Before the crew can withdraw, the East Spur comes down. Six survive the collapse, including Leena Orr, the carpenter Iven Tallo, and a fourteen-year-old messenger. Marek's right hand is crushed. Leena's shoulder is dislocated. The way up is gone. Beyond the ruined tunnel is the Hearthhold, a buried district of kitchens, clinics, a school, and a pump gallery that must be watched in shifts. Its boundary keeper, Sefu Aran, will not open the gate just because six strangers are desperate. Its air engineer, Nera Oduya, will not call a room safe merely because its ceiling is still overhead. Nothing in the Hearthhold is given without a term: conditions said aloud, stop authorities named, consent asked room by room, every refusal entered in Dalla Sen's ledger. A term no one can refuse is not a term. Water rises. Air must be tested. A room can kill while it remains standing. Marek has always made plans that end in a signature. In the Hearthhold, a plan with a person at the end has already chosen the person, and the person chosen is the one who cannot say no. Above them, the Cartwright guild claims the inspection line. A custody order from Dael Harrow locks the surface door and freezes guild equipment. Iven's guild bond is suspended for signing a maintenance sheet instead of the guild's custody line. The Hearthhold does not exist to solve Marek's emergency. Its people have water to carry, children to teach, and reasons to refuse. To make a route that holds, Marek must build with people who can stop him: repair a pump in a flooded gallery, open a corridor only while the pump runs, ask thirty people to stand on a school floor to see whether it holds. His right hand will not close around a brass rule. His plans stop being certificates and become things other people can refuse. He is losing the use of the hand that draws, the authority to sign, and the belief that a plan is a promise. What he has instead is a room full of people who can refuse him, and a route that holds only because they can still say no.

Ines Vale is third archivist of the Tide Office in Greywake, where the Register lies chained in a cellar eight feet under the quay. He has ruled its lines for six years and knows the book does not predict the future. It holds. A page read at the turn tells how sure the writing hand was — steady, hesitant, borrowed — and takes a piece of the reader in payment: a room, an hour, his sister's voice. It also makes the reader a holder of the entry, and the book counts agreement, not truth. Tomorrow's birth leaf is already written. B. Tam of the Ropewalk, a girl, first turn. Beneath it, in the same unbroken hand: Four days. The ninth hour. The Custom House stair. The hand is his sister's, four years dead, and it does not stop. The day column says seven where the words say four. By noon someone who knew which page to take has cut it from the binding, and the only copy he can carry is the one he makes from memory, in his own hand, with no witness at its foot. Bess Tam is five months along, not due until the ninth week of winter. The Register has already given her child a birth and a death. The court gives him seven days to produce a record that contradicts it. If he cannot, it stands, and Greywake will have a dead child and an accident written in a clerk's hand. Bess asks him to enter her child's birth early, before anyone can write a death under it. He does, in his own hand, and the Register agrees with him. It is the first false attestation of his life. No entry may be struck but by the Keeper on a superior order, and there is no superior order in Greywake. Ismay Rooke, Keeper for twenty-one years, will not strike it. Ossick Vaunt, second archivist, signed the unwitnessed page the forger copied and now files a report that is entirely true and entirely useless. In Kelder, the Chancery of the Tide wants a schedule of every unwitnessed page. One such page a year, for ninety-one years. Nine of them name people no one can produce: no household, no midwife, no burial, no claimant. Lives written into the book where no life was, and a town that believed it did the rest. A keep has no witness column. It can only be answered aloud, in a room, with a clerk writing down every voice and a living name at the foot of the leaf that is not the reader's — a name held forever. He has a copy nobody will attest, a grey print under his thumbnail, and a coast of strangers whose names he has no right to spend. The book does not need to be right. It only needs to be believed.

Aren Kest is a bridgewright in the fen town of Merefen, a road warden paid a shilling a day to read a load path. At thirty-two he buys a cracked Bellweather bell for two pence. The bell is an anchor. The trade calls this oathcraft: a promise made to an anchor. A working needs four parts: an anchor, a bound, a counterweight, and a witness. A road is two ends, a date, and a person at each end who has agreed to be there. Aren has the first three and no witness when he rings it and steps through. Bellweather is a city of four thousand, with a four-hundred-foot arch and a washing line over the crown. The Crown says the fever took it eleven years ago, and its own maps leave the city out. It buried two hundred and eleven and kept the ledger. A sealed writ was tendered by Edric Hunn, marshal. Aren comes home nine days late with a fever, a black roadmark across his left palm, and a missing line from a childhood song. Merefen bills him eleven marks and four pence. His brother Tovan signs as witness, then does not ask where he goes. Mara Vey, keeper of the Bellweather Claims Archive, faces a renewal date that will turn every claim into a rumor, and she has no authority to stop it. She needs a sworn tradesman's account of the bell; Aren needs a court to hear him. Magistrate Lysa Fenn accepts the exhibit and refuses the road. Against them are the Crown's finding that nothing survived and the marshal's office. A registration office offers Aren a district, a clerk, eleven marks a year, and a sealed record of himself if he closes the eastern paths. He refuses. He does not know how to close a road and will not learn. The work costs him. A footbridge in a county not on any map takes his leg; he walks with a stick. A crossing of twenty-three days costs twenty-six at home, and the error grows with the work. He refuses to let the leg be measured, because a figure becomes a survey. Roads do not reset. Bellweather goes on without him: tolls taken, bells rung by other hands. The County of Ash keeps a List of Persons to be Struck; a man at a kiln is alive and cannot be found. Every crossing leaves people who remember what he promised, and every promise is witnessed by someone who could have said no. He cannot undo a crossing, only go back. To keep the roads open, Aren pays with his leg, his brother's trust, and the days the crossings take from him. The question is not whether a man can walk into another country. It is what he owes the people still there when he leaves.

Milo Rook is a surveyor of record at the Civic Atlas Office in Alder Quay, a man paid to keep the route room's timetables honest. The reprint that comes off the press this Tuesday is wrong in a way no printer can fix. On Line 7, between Quayside and Ferryman's Rise, it lists a stop at 4:17. The stop is Bellwether Lane, a platform withdrawn six years earlier. The sheet gives the stop forty-one seconds of dwell on a schedule with no slack, and the Central Atlas has no such stop at all. The old platform register has the name, and the closure order bears Orrin Sable's signature. The city runs on a rule the timetable does not print: erased places do not vanish. A seam is a hole where two accounts of a place do not agree. A route can be made through one, but it needs a threshold, a turn, a witness, a return, and a count held by a person, not a box. A route that is drawn, watched, written down, and believed becomes a used route. A used route is a real one, and on this alignment the flood water will follow it. Every crossing costs Milo a route out of his own memory. The loss is not dramatic; it is clerical. He can still describe the way to the office, but he cannot find it. Already, there are only two rooms in the city he can reach without being led, and one of them is at the end of his own stairs. He has copied the route home into his field book after every survey since he was nineteen. Now he needs someone to walk him home. Against him are the Registry of Continuance, which would rather close a file than open a street, and Survey Enforcement, which can measure a place and file it as a minor seam with no persons affected. Sable does not deny the seam. He argues that Milo's map has made it legible, that a believed route is a used route, and that the water will take the service door out of the flood wall and go into the low streets. Mara Quill, an advocate, wants Bellwether Lane back on the street index. The residents of Cedar Court want to stop being legally no one. But a name on the street index is what the clinic, the school, and the post read, and restoring the name would stop the relocation money. Cedar Court can have an address or the money, not both. Milo has spent nineteen years drawing routes for other people. Now he must decide how much of his own memory he is willing to spend proving that a street the city has already forgotten is still there, and whether the people who live on it can survive being found.

The Ninth Furnace has never been run hot. Cinderhold keeps it at its lowest lawful bank and meters its warmth out by consent. The cut order is nailed to a pump-house wall, and the fourth clause of every consent says a chill may follow and the office accepts no notice of it. Bram Ostler is nineteen, a third-rank reader on the second bench of the Ninth House. He can read heat and direction off iron and people. Not intent, not words, not images, not memories: heat, and the direction it runs. A person is a small thing with a centre in it, and a lie is the cold place in it. A glance takes days off the mark over his sternum. A working gauge takes a season. A deep read takes a year or more, and none of it comes back. When a proof charge comes in short on sound iron, Bram follows the cold with a lamp and a stub of chalk, because looking is free, and finds a branch cut into the Crane Row run, the block still on the cut list, and crates stencilled SPENT going out along the wharf road with warm rods inside. Someone is selling the city's warmth as spent iron. The guild does not act on a story. It wants a reading that can be paid for, consented to, witnessed, and entered in a book. Guild law is exact: a reading that spends more than the reader holds is not a finding. It is a hole, and the house does not accept holes. The Keeper of the Gauge believes him and tells him why belief is not enough. The Warden's office counts consents. The Council of Nine is nine chairs sealed in the charter. A holder has no office and no instrument for an exception. The loss is spread across the ring, block by block, and there is no person in this city who is the ring. Bram is barred from the Gauge House and his account is nearly empty. Wren Sallow, the furnacewright who has risked her own name for him, cannot take the signature back. The proof he needs is a held reading of a place, which is unlawful anywhere and costs more seasons than he has left. The Long Cold is coming, Crane Row is still on the cut list, and the only proof the house takes is a reading paid out of a man's own seasons. Bram can find the hole for nothing. To make Cinderhold believe it, he must spend the little warmth he has left.

Marek Vale is a third-grade clerk in the Chamber of Accounts at Bell Stair. The Tower lends what people cannot wait for — a year of youth, a year of a trade, a season's recovery — and takes the pledge out of the future. Every loan is written in five parts: need, pledge, scope, witness, settlement. A loan missing one is not void. It is false-witnessed, and the Tower goes looking for a person to carry it. Marek's job is to read the receipt against the sealed terms and sign it, or find the clause that stops it. Then a Tallow Ward water assessment reaches his bench with a false recital, eleven unsigned sureties, and a settlement that must be sealed before the twelfth or there is no gate and the low kitchens go under. Marek finds a remedy in the margin of the Tower's founding page: a standing hold, held by the clerk of record, an office vacant since the third century. It moves the settlement to the end of the year. It does not cancel the debt. It puts the delay in the clerk's own yearline. He holds it for six bells. At the sixth, the collection walks the chain to the living signature at the foot of the entry: Ondra Kelb, twenty, three weeks in the post, whose hand goes still. By morning there is a new mark on Marek's forearm, a ruled line with four notches, not a wound. Suspended and unpaid, Marek keeps reading. The paper leads him out of Tallow to Rainmarket, where a seed cooperative's loan favours the sowing season and makes the whole low ground bear its failure. It leads him to the Sable Compact, a claims house that buys and bundles paper until the last name on the chain is a district. It leads him back to Hesper Rann, the supervisor whose lie kept Tallow above water. His brother Tomas is working a vigor loan their mother witnessed, and his hands are going. The Trust wants a villain who fits in a box. The Compact wants the blank line in the Tower's oldest ledger, a claim with nobody behind it. Marek wants a room where a person can ask what they are standing in before the collection comes. He can read a page by touch, which is how he finds the clause nobody else can see. The reading costs him a headache, a taste of iron, a hand that shakes. The holds cost more. Every delay has to be carried somewhere, and the Tower's answer is always the same: put the cost on a district, a ward, a class, and find a person to sign. Marek is one clerk with a notched arm and a vacant office. He can hold a settlement for six bells. The Tower has an answer for the seventh.
